status: Drafted via direct single-pass analysis grounded in the real extracted Geneva Bible verse text (Assets/Resources/Verses/Geneva/wisdom_of_solomon_45.json); not yet adversarially fact-checked by a second pass.
notes: Wisdom of Solomon is a philosophical/wisdom treatise rather than a straightforward narrative, and this shaped the whole tier structure. Roughly its first third (ch.1-6) is direct moral address - an unnamed royal teacher (traditionally Solomon, though the text itself never once uses that name) contrasting the ungodly's hedonistic, fatalist reasoning with the eternal reward of the righteous, then turning to warn kings and judges specifically. The middle section (ch.6-9) is Solomon's own extended love-poem to and prayer for personified Wisdom ("she"), who is developed as a fully embodied divine figure in her own right - not a minor theme, but arguably the book's central character, so she gets her own major manager tier rather than being folded into a generic "wisdom" law tier. Chapter 10 is a remarkable extended survey of Wisdom's action across the whole Genesis-to-Exodus sweep of Israel's history, told entirely through unnamed periphrasis: "the first formed father of the world," "the righteous man's course by a poor piece of wood," "a righteous man was sold" - every single historical figure (Adam, Cain, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Lot, Lot's wife, Jacob, Esau, Joseph, Joseph's brothers, Potiphar's wife, Moses, Aaron) is identified purely through unmistakable descriptive detail matching their Genesis/Exodus story, never by name - a genuine, deliberate stylistic riddle-device running through the whole book, not an extraction artifact, and flagged here rather than silently resolved or invented. Chapters 11-19 shift into a sustained "measure for measure" argument about the Exodus plagues (Egypt punished through the very things it worshipped or did, Israel provided for by the same means), interrupted by an extended, vivid critique of idol-worship (ch.13-15, from a carpenter's crooked offcut to a potter's identical clay) that is law/theme material rather than narrative and is credited to Solomon as teacher. The climax (ch.18-19) depicts God's own "all-powerful word" acting directly as a warrior on the Passover night, alongside Aaron's own vivid, personally-embodied incense-intercession that halts a plague (18:20-25, matching Numbers 16) - distinct enough from Moses' own leadership material to warrant Aaron his own manager tier. Because this book gives no family/genealogical detail for any of the Genesis/Exodus figures it alludes to, every genealogy field here is left empty by design - the real genealogies for Adam, Cain, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Lot, Jacob, Esau, Joseph, Moses, and Aaron already exist in the fully-built KJV Genesis/Exodus Character Index and are deliberately not re-derived or duplicated here. This book does not exist in the KJV canon at all (it is Apocrypha, unique to canons like the Geneva Bible's own Apocrypha section), so none of its ids or content overlap with or alter any existing KJV entry.

characters.name: Solomon (unnamed narrator)

genealogy.father: Implied to be David via "worthy of my father's throne" (9:12), though "David" is never named in this book's text either.

verses.note: Opens the book addressing "ye that be judges of the earth," urging them to seek the Lord in singleness of heart - the teaching king's own voice.
Directly instructs "O princes" and declares he will trace Wisdom's nature "from the beginning of creation" without envy or concealment.
Confesses his own ordinary mortality: moulded in the womb like any man, born with the same first wailing cry.
"I called upon God, and there came to me a spirit of wisdom. I preferred her before sceptres and thrones."
Sought Wisdom out from his youth "to take her for my bride"; realizes he cannot possess her except God gives her, and so turns to prayer.
Recalls being "chosen... before my brethren to be king" and commanded to build the sanctuary and altar (the Temple); prays to be "worthy of my father's throne."

funFacts: Never once actually named "Solomon" in the text - his identity is signaled entirely through royal, Temple-building, and "my father's throne" details that only fit David's son.

characters.name: Wisdom (personified)

verses.note: "Wisdom is radiant and fadeth not away... she goeth about, herself seeking them that are worthy of her."
The book's great catalogue of her nature: "a spirit quick of understanding, holy... an effulgence from everlasting light, an unspotted mirror of the working of God."
"She, being one, hath power to do all things... maketh men friends of God and prophets."
"She reacheth from one end of the world to the other with full strength, and ordereth all things graciously"; "the Sovereign Lord of all loved her."
Present beside God "when thou wast making the world"; sent down from the holy heavens to toil beside Solomon and guide him.
Her first historical act: guards Adam and delivers him out of his own transgression, giving him dominion.
Delivers "a holy people" from oppressors and "entered into the soul of a servant of the Lord" (Moses), withstanding terrible kings.

funFacts: Described entirely in feminine, personal terms ("she") - one of the most developed personifications of Wisdom anywhere in scripture, called a "breath of the power of God" (7:25) rather than a mere abstract quality.

characters.name: The First Formed Father (Adam)

verses.note: "Wisdom guarded to the end the first formed father of the world, that was created alone, and delivered him out of his own transgression, and gave him strength to get dominion over all things."

funFacts: Called only "the first formed father of the world, that was created alone" - his name never actually appears anywhere in this book.

verses.note: "When an unrighteous man fell away from her in his anger, he perished himself in the rage wherewith he slew his brother." Note: unnamed in the text; identified via the unmistakable fratricide detail immediately following the Adam reference.

characters.name: The Righteous Man of the Flood (Noah)

verses.note: "When for his cause the earth was drowning with a flood, Wisdom again saved it, guiding the righteous man's course by a poor piece of wood."

characters.name: The Righteous Man of the Confounded Nations (Abraham)

verses.note: "When nations consenting together in wickedness had been confounded [Babel], Wisdom knew the righteous man, and preserved him blameless unto God, and kept him strong when his heart yearned toward his child [the binding of Isaac]." Note: unnamed; identified via the Babel-confusion-then-child-testing sequence.
The unnamed "child" toward whom Abraham's heart yearned; read against Genesis 22, this is Isaac at the Akedah. Not named in the text itself.

characters.name: The Righteous Man Who Fled the Fire (Lot)

verses.note: "While the ungodly were perishing, wisdom delivered a righteous man, when he fled from the fire that descended out of heaven on Pentapolis [the cities of the plain]." His wickedness's smoking waste, and "plants bearing fair fruit that cometh not to ripeness," still witness to it.
"A disbelieving soul hath a memorial there, a pillar of salt still standing." Note: unnamed in the text; identified via the unmistakable pillar-of-salt detail from Genesis 19.

characters.name: The Fugitive from His Brother's Wrath (Jacob)

verses.note: "When a righteous man was a fugitive from a brother's wrath, wisdom guided him in straight paths; she shewed him God's kingdom [the ladder vision at Bethel]... she guarded him from enemies... that he might know that godliness is more powerful than all."
The unnamed "brother" whose "wrath" Jacob fled. Not named in the text itself; identified via the fraternal-flight detail matching Genesis 27.

characters.name: The Righteous Man Who Was Sold (Joseph)

verses.note: "When a righteous man was sold, wisdom forsook him not... she went down with him into a dungeon, and in bonds she left him not, till she brought him the sceptre of a kingdom, and authority over those that dealt tyrannously with him; she shewed them also to be false that had mockingly accused him, and gave him eternal glory."
The unnamed party who sold him. Note: treated as one collective entry since the text does not individualize their actions; matches Genesis 37.
"She shewed them also to be false that had mockingly accused him." Note: the unnamed accuser; identified via the false-accusation detail matching Genesis 39.

characters.name: The Servant of the Lord (Moses)

verses.note: "Wisdom delivered a holy people and a blameless seed from a nation of oppressors. She entered into the soul of a servant of the Lord, and withstood terrible kings in wonders and signs."
Wisdom becomes the people's "covering in the day-time, and a flame of stars through the night," brings them over the Red Sea, and drowns their enemies.
"She prospered their works in the hand of a holy prophet"; the people cry out in thirst and are given water "out of the flinty rock."
Under his leadership the people receive "angels' food to eat" (the manna) from heaven.
The pillar of fire guides Israel's "unknown journey" through the wilderness.

funFacts: Called only "a servant of the Lord" and "a holy prophet" - like every other figure in ch.10-19, Moses is never once named in this book's own text.

verses.note: During a plague in the wilderness, "a blameless man hasted to be their champion: bringing the weapon of his own ministry, even prayer and the propitiation of incense, he withstood the indignation, and set an end to the calamity."
"He overcame the anger, not by strength of body... but by word did he subdue the minister of punishment"; stands between the dead and the living to halt the advancing plague.

"Upon his long highpriestly robe was the whole world, and the glories of the fathers were upon the graving of the four rows of precious stones, and thy majesty was upon the diadem of his head." Note: unnamed in the text; identified as Aaron via the high-priestly breastplate imagery (Exodus 28) and the incense plague-stopping act, which matches Numbers 16:46-48.

characters.name: The Ungodly and the Righteous
characters.purpose: A sustained moral contrast, cast partly as the wicked's own recorded reasoning (their hedonist, fatalist speech in ch.2) and partly as Solomon's own teaching: death was not created by God but entered through the devil's envy; the ungodly's short life of pleasure and oppression of the righteous ends in the ruin they invited, while the souls of the righteous - however despised, childless, or cut off in this life - are in God's hand and cannot be touched by torment.

verses.note: "God made not death; neither delighteth he when the living perish... for he created all things that they might have being."
"Ungodly men by their hands and their words called death unto them... they made a covenant with him."
The ungodly's own reasoning: "short and sorrowful is our life... let us fill ourselves with costly wine and perfumes... let us crown ourselves with rosebuds, before they be withered."
Their resolve to oppress the righteous poor and put "the righteous man" to a shameful test and death, "because he is of disservice to us."
"God created man for incorruption... but by the envy of the devil death entered into the world."
"The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and no torment shall touch them... they shall judge nations, and have dominion over peoples."
The blessing of the barren woman and the faithful eunuch, "undefiled" and having "wrought no lawless deed."
At the judgement, the wicked stand before the man they once mocked, confessing "we fools accounted his life madness."
"The righteous live for ever... he shall put on righteousness as a breastplate" - the closing armor-of-God passage.

characters.name: The Judgment of Kings and Rulers
characters.purpose: A direct warning to earthly rulers, framed as a deliberate echo of the book's own opening address to "judges of the earth": dominion is lent by God, not owned outright, and the powerful will be searched out more strictly than the humble precisely because more was entrusted to them.

verses.note: "Hear therefore, ye kings, and understand... your dominion was given you from the Lord... who shall search out your works."
"Awfully and swiftly shall he come upon you... mighty men shall be searched out mightily."
"Unto you therefore, O princes, are my words, that ye may learn wisdom and fall not from the right way."
"If therefore ye delight in thrones and sceptres, ye princes of peoples, honour wisdom, that ye may reign for ever."

characters.name: The Folly of Idols
characters.purpose: A two-part critique of idolatry: first, the more forgivable error of mistaking the beauty of created things (fire, wind, stars) for gods; then the far less excusable folly of worshipping objects human hands themselves carved, illustrated by an extended parable of a carpenter who burns half a crooked log for fuel and carves the leftover knot into a household god - closing with a potter's-clay parable making the same point about self-deifying craftsmen, and transitioning into Egypt's own animal-worship.

verses.note: "All men by nature were but vain who had no perception of God... they thought [fire, wind, stars] to be gods that rule the world."
"Miserable were they... who called them gods which are works of men's hands... a crooked piece of wood and full of knots, carveth it with the diligence of his idleness."
The idol-worshipper prays to the lifeless image "for health... for life... for a good journey," to that which cannot so much as move a step.

"The devising of idols was the beginning of fornication"; traces the origin of idol-worship to a grieving father's image of a dead child, later formalized "as a law" by princes and flattery of absent kings.
The moral collapse that follows idol-worship: "blood and murder, theft and deceit... confusion of sex, disorder in marriage."
The potter's parable: "out of the same clay doth he fashion both the vessels that minister to clean uses, and those of a contrary sort," yet still moulds "a vain god out of the same clay."
Turns specifically to Egypt: "most foolish were they all... who oppressed [Israel]... they even accounted all the idols of the nations to be gods."

characters.name: Egypt's Plagues, Israel's Providence
characters.purpose: Recounts, point by point, how Wisdom answered each of Egypt's own sins with a fitting judgement while providing for Israel's needs by the very same means - a sustained "measure for measure" argument that God's justice and mercy are two faces of the same providence.

verses.note: The Nile turned to clotted blood is contrasted with water from the rock; God tries His own people "as a father" while condemning Egypt "as a stern king."
Egypt's worship of "irrational reptiles and wretched vermin" is answered by a plague "of irrational creatures for vengeance."
Egypt is punished "through creatures like those which they worship," while Israel is given quails.
Fiery serpents afflict the wilderness camp; a bronze "token of salvation" is raised (Numbers 21), but the text is careful that it was God, not the token itself, who healed.
Hail and fire together punish Egypt in an unnatural reversal of the elements' usual opposition.
The manna, "bread ready for their use... from heaven," tempers itself to every man's taste and melts in sunlight to teach gratitude and early rising.
The plague of darkness upon Egypt: terror, phantoms, and paralysis, "a heavy night" set against the light enjoyed everywhere else in the world.

characters.name: The Passover Night and the Reordered Creation
characters.purpose: The book's climax: on the night of the first Passover, God's own "all-powerful word" descends directly as a warrior to bring death to Egypt's firstborn while Israel's households keep the appointed rites in safety; the closing chapter widens this into a meditation on all creation being reordered - fire, water, and the sea itself changing their nature - to serve God's people during the Exodus, ending with a comparison of Egypt's cruelty to guests against the ancient wickedness of Sodom. Deliberately left unattributed to any human manager, since the text specifically credits God's own "word" acting directly, not a human intermediary.

verses.note: Egypt's plan "to slay the babes of the holy ones" is turned back onto their own children.
Israel's "holy children of good men offered sacrifice in secret" and kept the Passover together in faith.
"Thine all-powerful word leaped from heaven out of the royal throne, a stern warrior... it filled all things with death."
The Red Sea crossing: "the whole creation... was fashioned again anew," dry land rising up out of what before was water.
Egypt's cruelty to Israel as guests is set beside "the men of Sodom," who likewise "received not the strangers" (cross-referencing Lot's own tier).
The elements "changing their order one with another," fire and water exchanging their natural powers to protect the righteous.

genealogyLists.note: This book gives zero genealogical detail (parents/spouses/children) for any of the eleven historical figures it alludes to in ch.10 - Adam, Cain, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Lot, Lot's Wife, Jacob, Esau, Joseph, Joseph's Brothers, Potiphar's Wife - plus Moses and Aaron in ch.11-19. Full genealogies for the ones with discrete KJV entries already exist in the KJV Genesis/Exodus Character Index (ids roughly: adam, cain, noah, abraham, isaac, lot, jacob, esau, joseph, moses, aaron) and were deliberately not re-derived or duplicated here.

unnamedFigures.note: Every historical figure in this chapter is identified only by unmistakable descriptive periphrasis, never by proper name - a genuine literary device of the book itself, not a gap in this extraction. The same is true of Moses and Aaron later in the book (ch.11-19).

solomonAttribution.note: The narrator/speaker is never once named "Solomon" anywhere in the text; the attribution rests entirely on the book's traditional title plus strong internal clues (chosen king before his brethren, commanded to build the Temple, praying to be worthy of "my father's throne").
